To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we can accelerate the PAM SWAP phase by a factor of k by using a small amount of extra memory, and that we can further accelerate this by performing multiple swaps per iteration.

(1) PAM, CLARANS, and CLARA can be accelerated by a factor of up to k with only a minor quality loss; (2) this acceleration is possible at the cost of O(k) memory; (3) we propose a novel, fast implementation of k-medoids, called PAM++; (4) PAM++ is faster than k-means, k-prototypes, and k-modes on non-Euclidean, real-world data;
we have developed faster k-medoids algorithms that find the same results and are applicable to larger data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
speeding up the PAM algorithm, which is one of the most widely used clustering algorithms.
the following questions: 1. Can we improve the performance of PAM, CLARANS, and CLARA? 2. What are the trade-offs of the proposed modifications? 3. How can we best apply the modified algorithms?

the following questions: How to speed up the PAM, and related algorithms, without sacrificing quality? Can we speed up the algorithms further by allowing more than one swap in each iteration? How do these algorithms scale with k?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our modifications to PAM, CLARANS, and CLARA, are very useful for practitioners, and can be used to speed up the algorithms by up to a factor of 200.

PAM is not the best clustering algorithm, but it is still a very good algorithm that has been used in many applications and that has the advantage that the algorithm is easy to understand and implement.

PAM is a very good algorithm for clustering data in the presence of arbitrary distances, and the proposed modifications allow to run it on data sets with hundreds of thousands of instances and hundreds of clusters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have improved the run time complexity of k-medoids clustering by a factor of k.
our modifications can speed up the PAM, the CLARA and the CLARANS algorithms by up to 1000 times.
we can now cluster large non-Euclidean datasets with PAM, CLARANS and CLARA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
by storing O(k) extra values we can accelerate the PAM algorithm by O(k) without compromising the results.

the PAM,CLARA,CLARANS algorithms are not only useful for clustering data in Euclidean spaces, but can also be used to find medoid-based clusters on arbitrary dissimilarities, and can be sped up by a large factor.
we can achieve a speedup of O(k) for the PAM algorithm, and even higher for other algorithms, by only storing O(k) extra values.
